title: JVM Architecture & Java Platform
overview: Java source code is compiled into platform-independent bytecode. A Java Virtual Machine implementation loads and executes that bytecode on a particular operating system and processor. The Java platform separates the language, development tools and runtime execution environment.

sections.heading: Compilation and execution
sections.body: The usual flow is .java source → javac compiler → .class bytecode → class loading and verification → execution by the JVM. The interpreter can execute bytecode, while a Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler may compile frequently used code paths to native machine code. The exact optimisation strategy is JVM-implementation dependent.

sections.heading: JDK, JRE and JVM
sections.body: The JVM is the execution engine and runtime specification/implementation. A traditional JRE bundles the JVM with runtime libraries. The JDK contains development tools such as javac and javadoc plus the runtime components needed to run Java programs. Modern JDK distributions may package runtime components differently, but the conceptual distinction remains useful.

sections.heading: Runtime areas
sections.body: The heap stores objects and arrays and is shared by threads. Each thread has its own Java virtual machine stack containing frames for method invocations. A frame holds local variables, an operand stack and bookkeeping information. The program counter register is per-thread. Class metadata is represented in the method area conceptually; HotSpot uses Metaspace for class metadata.

sections.heading: Common misconceptions
sections.body: Java bytecode is not native machine code. Java is not automatically immune to memory leaks; objects can remain reachable unintentionally. The JVM specification describes required behaviour, while implementation details such as garbage collectors and JIT heuristics can differ.

title: Java Basics, Variables & Scope
overview: A Java program is organised around classes, interfaces, records and other declarations. Variables have types and scopes, and their lifetime depends on where and how they are declared.

sections.heading: Variable categories
sections.body: A local variable is declared in a method, constructor or block and must be definitely assigned before it is read. An instance field belongs to an object and receives a default value when the object is created. A static field belongs to the class rather than to each object. Parameters are local to the invoked method or constructor.

sections.heading: Scope and shadowing
sections.body: A local variable is visible from its declaration to the end of its enclosing block, subject to Java's declaration rules. A local variable can shadow a field with the same name; this.field refers to the current object's field. Static context has no this reference.

sections.heading: Source structure and JavaDoc
sections.body: A compilation unit can contain package and import declarations followed by top-level type declarations. JavaDoc comments use /** ... */ and can be processed by the javadoc tool to create API documentation. Ordinary // and /* ... */ comments are not JavaDoc documentation comments.

sections.heading: Java 17 baseline
sections.body: The supplied course guidelines specify Java 17 LTS as the standard for sessions, lab work and evaluation. Examples in this platform avoid requiring features introduced after Java 17.

title: Object-Oriented Programming Foundations
overview: Object-oriented programming models software using objects that combine state and behaviour. A class defines a type and a construction blueprint; an object is a runtime instance of a class.

sections.heading: Four core ideas
sections.body: Encapsulation groups data and operations while controlling access. Abstraction exposes essential behaviour while hiding implementation detail. Inheritance enables a subtype to derive from a superclass. Polymorphism allows a common supertype reference to refer to objects with different runtime types and dispatch overridden instance methods dynamically.

sections.heading: Class and object
sections.body: Fields represent object or class state. Methods define behaviour. Constructors initialise newly created objects and are invoked with new (except special mechanisms such as deserialization or reflection). A reference variable stores a reference value; it is not the object itself.

sections.heading: Design guidance
sections.body: Prefer clear responsibilities and composition when a type does not represent a genuine is-a relationship. Encapsulation is stronger when fields are private and state changes are controlled through methods that preserve invariants.

title: Data Types, Wrappers & Operators
overview: Java is statically typed. Its eight primitive types are boolean, byte, short, int, long, char, float and double. Reference types include classes, interfaces, arrays and enums.

sections.heading: Conversions
sections.body: Widening primitive conversions generally move to a type with a broader range, such as int to long. Narrowing conversions require an explicit cast and may lose information. The compiler applies binary numeric promotion in many arithmetic expressions. Integer division truncates toward zero.

sections.heading: Wrapper classes
sections.body: Each primitive has a corresponding wrapper class, such as Integer for int and Boolean for boolean. Autoboxing converts a primitive to its wrapper; unboxing converts the wrapper to a primitive. Unboxing a null wrapper throws NullPointerException. Wrapper objects are immutable.

sections.heading: Operators
sections.body: Arithmetic operators include +, -, *, / and %. Relational operators compare values. && and || short-circuit; & and | can also operate on booleans but evaluate both operands. Bitwise operators operate on integral values. == compares primitive values or reference identity; equals is a method whose meaning is defined by the class.

sections.heading: Precedence
sections.body: Parentheses are the clearest way to make evaluation order explicit. Unary operators, multiplicative operators, additive operators, relational operators, equality operators, logical operators and assignment operators have different precedence levels. Associativity determines grouping when precedence is equal.

title: Control Statements
overview: Control statements determine which statements execute and how often loops repeat. Branches and loops should be designed with explicit conditions and termination behaviour.

sections.heading: Selection
sections.body: if and if-else select a path based on a boolean expression. A traditional switch supports selected integral, enum, String and certain wrapper selector types; case labels must be compatible constant labels. A traditional switch statement can fall through unless break or another transfer statement exits the switch.

sections.heading: Iteration
sections.body: A for loop is convenient when initialisation, condition and update belong together. A while loop checks its condition before each iteration. A do-while loop executes its body at least once because the condition is checked afterward.

sections.heading: break and continue
sections.body: break exits the nearest enclosing loop or switch; a labelled break can exit a labelled enclosing statement. continue skips the remainder of the current loop iteration and proceeds to the next iteration, with the exact update/condition sequence determined by the loop form.

title: Packages, Imports & Java Tools
overview: Packages organise related types, provide namespaces and participate in access control. Imports allow source files to use simple names for accessible types.

sections.heading: Package and import rules
sections.body: A package declaration, when present, appears before imports and type declarations. An import does not copy a class into the current file; it makes a type or static member available by a shorter name. A fully qualified name can be used without an import. java.lang types are implicitly available by simple name.

sections.heading: Access and directories
sections.body: Package-private members are accessible to code in the same package. protected access includes same-package access and qualifying subclass access. Public top-level types are generally placed in source files whose names match the public type. Package names are conventionally lowercase and map to directory paths.

sections.heading: Tools
sections.body: javac compiles Java source. java launches a class or module. javadoc generates API documentation from JavaDoc comments. jar creates and manages archive files. Tool options vary by JDK release; use the JDK 17 documentation for this course baseline.

title: Arrays
overview: An array is a fixed-length object whose elements have one declared component type. Array indices start at zero, and the length is available through the length field.

sections.heading: Creation and defaults
sections.body: An array variable may be declared with type[] syntax. Creating an array with new allocates its elements and initialises them to default values: numeric primitives to zero, boolean to false and reference elements to null. An array's length cannot be changed after creation.

sections.heading: Bounds and dimensions
sections.body: For an array of length n, valid indices are 0 through n-1. An invalid index causes ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. A two-dimensional Java array is an array of arrays; rows can have different lengths (a jagged array).

sections.heading: Utilities
sections.body: java.util.Arrays provides helpers such as sort, binarySearch, equals, fill, copyOf and toString. binarySearch assumes the searched array is sorted according to the relevant ordering; otherwise its result is not reliable.

title: String & StringBuilder
overview: String represents immutable character sequences. StringBuilder represents a mutable sequence and is useful when many modifications are performed by one thread.

sections.heading: Immutability and equality
sections.body: Methods such as concat, replace and toUpperCase return a String result; they do not mutate the original String. equals compares character content. == compares reference identity. String literals may be interned, but code should not rely on reference equality for content comparison.

sections.heading: StringBuilder
sections.body: StringBuilder supports append, insert, delete, replace and reverse while modifying the same builder object. Its methods are not synchronised. StringBuffer offers synchronised methods when that older thread-safe mutable sequence is required.

sections.heading: Choosing a representation
sections.body: Use String for ordinary immutable text values. Use StringBuilder for repeated concatenation in a loop or many sequential modifications. The compiler may optimise simple concatenation expressions, but explicit builders make repeated mutation intent clear.

title: Methods, Constructors & Encapsulation
overview: Methods define operations, parameters receive argument values, and constructors initialise objects. Encapsulation controls how state is accessed and changed.

sections.heading: Pass-by-value
sections.body: Java is always pass-by-value. For a primitive parameter, the value is copied. For an object parameter, the reference value is copied, so the method can mutate the referenced object but cannot reassign the caller's variable. Reassigning the parameter does not change the caller's reference.

sections.heading: Overloading and constructors
sections.body: Overloaded methods share a name but have different parameter lists. Return type alone cannot distinguish overloads. Constructors have the class name and no return type. If no constructor is declared, the compiler can provide a default no-argument constructor. Once any constructor is declared, that implicit default is not supplied.

sections.heading: Access and immutability
sections.body: private is the most restrictive ordinary member access; package-private has no modifier; protected adds subclass access; public is broadly accessible subject to module and type accessibility. An immutable class prevents observable state changes after construction, commonly by making fields private and final, avoiding setters, and defensively copying mutable inputs and outputs.

title: Inheritance, Abstract Classes & Interfaces
overview: Inheritance expresses an is-a relationship. Abstract classes and interfaces define contracts and shared structure, but they serve different design purposes.

sections.heading: Classes
sections.body: A Java class can extend one direct superclass. Constructors are not inherited. A subclass constructor invokes a superclass constructor, explicitly or through an implicit super() call where permitted. Object is the root superclass of ordinary classes.

sections.heading: Abstract classes
sections.body: An abstract class cannot be instantiated directly. It may contain abstract methods, concrete methods, fields and constructors. A concrete subclass must implement inherited abstract methods unless it is also abstract.

sections.heading: Interfaces
sections.body: A class can implement multiple interfaces. An interface may declare abstract methods, default methods, static methods, constants and private helper methods (Java 9+). Interface fields are implicitly public static final. Interface methods can define a capability contract without forcing a class inheritance hierarchy.

title: Polymorphism, Casting & Overriding
overview: A supertype reference can refer to a subtype object. For overridden instance methods, the runtime object's class determines which implementation executes.

sections.heading: Reference type and runtime type
sections.body: The declared reference type controls which members are accessible at compile time. The actual object's runtime type controls dynamic dispatch for overridden instance methods. Static methods are hidden rather than overridden, and fields are resolved using the declared reference type.

sections.heading: Casting
sections.body: Upcasting a subtype reference to a supertype is safe and usually implicit. Downcasting requires an explicit cast and succeeds only when the object is compatible with the target type; otherwise ClassCastException is thrown. instanceof can test compatibility before casting.

sections.heading: Overriding rules
sections.body: An overriding method must have a compatible signature and cannot reduce visibility. It may use a covariant return type and cannot broaden checked exceptions beyond those permitted by the overridden method. @Override helps the compiler detect accidental non-overrides.

title: Exception Handling
overview: Exceptions represent abnormal conditions and transfer control to a matching handler or propagate to the caller. Java distinguishes checked exceptions, unchecked exceptions and errors.

sections.heading: Hierarchy
sections.body: Throwable is the root. Exception and Error extend Throwable. RuntimeException is an Exception subclass. Checked exceptions are subject to catch-or-declare rules; RuntimeException subclasses and Error subclasses are unchecked.

sections.heading: try, catch and finally
sections.body: A matching catch handles a thrown exception. More specific catch clauses must appear before broader clauses. finally normally executes when control leaves the try statement, including many exceptional paths; process termination or abrupt VM failure can prevent it. A return in finally can suppress an earlier return or exception and is generally discouraged.

sections.heading: throw, throws and custom exceptions
sections.body: throw actually throws a Throwable instance. throws declares possible checked exceptions in a method signature. A custom checked exception usually extends Exception; a custom unchecked exception usually extends RuntimeException. Choose based on whether callers are expected to recover and handle the condition.

sections.heading: Try-with-resources
sections.body: Resources implementing AutoCloseable can be declared in a try-with-resources header. They are closed automatically in reverse declaration order. If both the body and close operation fail, the body exception remains primary and close failures are recorded as suppressed exceptions.

title: Enums, Autoboxing, Generics & Collections
overview: Enums model a fixed set of named constants. Generics provide compile-time type safety for classes, interfaces and methods that operate on types supplied by callers.

sections.heading: Enums
sections.body: An enum is a special class with a fixed set of instances declared as enum constants. Enums can have fields, constructors and methods. Enum constructors are not invoked directly by client code. values() returns the declared constants in declaration order; valueOf(String) looks up a constant by its exact name.

sections.heading: Generics
sections.body: A type such as List<String> constrains elements to String at compile time. Generic type information is largely erased at runtime, so new T(), instanceof List<String> and generic array creation are restricted. Use bounded type parameters when operations require a capability such as Comparable.

sections.heading: Collections overview
sections.body: The Collection interface is the root of List, Set and Queue families. Map is part of the Collections Framework but is not a subtype of Collection. Lists preserve positional order and allow duplicates; sets enforce uniqueness according to their equality/ordering rules; maps associate keys with values.

title: Functional Programming & Lambdas
overview: Java functional programming uses functional interfaces and lambda expressions to pass behaviour as values, often for collection processing and callbacks.

sections.heading: Functional interfaces
sections.body: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method (ignoring methods corresponding to public Object methods). It may also contain default and static methods. @FunctionalInterface documents intent and asks the compiler to enforce the rule.

sections.heading: Core java.util.function types
sections.body: Predicate<T> tests a value and returns boolean. Function<T,R> transforms a T into R. Consumer<T> accepts a T and returns no result. Supplier<T> provides a value without an input. Primitive specialisations can reduce boxing.

sections.heading: Lambda expressions
sections.body: A lambda implements the abstract method of a target functional interface. Parameter types can often be inferred from context. A lambda can capture local variables only when they are final or effectively final. Lambdas do not introduce a new this; this refers to the enclosing instance.

title: Collection Framework & Operations
overview: The Collections Framework provides interfaces and implementations for groups of objects. Choose data structures according to ordering, duplicates, lookup and update requirements.

sections.heading: Main abstractions
sections.body: List is ordered by position and permits duplicates. Set models uniqueness. Queue models elements awaiting processing. Map stores key/value associations and does not extend Collection. Iterable enables enhanced for iteration.

sections.heading: Common implementations
sections.body: ArrayList offers efficient indexed access and amortised append. LinkedList supports deque operations but indexed access is linear. HashSet and HashMap provide hash-based lookup with expected constant-time operations under good hash distribution. TreeSet and TreeMap maintain sorted order, generally with logarithmic operations.

sections.heading: Bulk operations
sections.body: forEach applies an action to elements. removeIf removes elements satisfying a Predicate. replaceAll transforms list elements using a UnaryOperator. Collections.sort sorts a list; List.sort is also available. Avoid structural modification of most collections during enhanced-for iteration unless using a supported iterator operation.

title: Streams & Stream API
overview: A Stream pipeline describes a sequence of operations over a data source. Streams are not storage containers and are generally consumed once.

sections.heading: Pipeline model
sections.body: A pipeline consists of a source, zero or more intermediate operations and a terminal operation. Intermediate operations such as filter, map, flatMap, distinct, sorted and limit are lazy. A terminal operation such as collect, reduce, count, forEach or a match operation triggers evaluation.

sections.heading: map versus flatMap
sections.body: map transforms each input element into one output element. flatMap transforms each input into a stream and flattens those produced streams into a single stream. flatMap is useful when each parent item has zero or more child items.

sections.heading: Reduction and primitive streams
sections.body: reduce combines elements into a result using an associative accumulation operation when parallel execution is possible. collect performs mutable reduction into a result container. IntStream, LongStream and DoubleStream provide primitive specialisations and operations such as sum, average and summary statistics, avoiding wrapper overhead in many cases.

sections.heading: Cautions
sections.body: Do not reuse a consumed stream. Prefer non-interfering, stateless pipeline functions. Parallel streams do not automatically make work faster; overhead, data size, ordering and shared mutable state matter.

title: Java Date-Time API
overview: The java.time API provides immutable, thread-safe types for dates, times, instants, durations, periods and formatting.

sections.heading: Choosing the type
sections.body: LocalDate represents a calendar date without a time zone. LocalTime represents a wall-clock time without a date or zone. LocalDateTime combines date and time without a zone. Instant represents a point on the UTC timeline. ZonedDateTime combines a date-time with a time zone.

sections.heading: Duration and Period
sections.body: Duration measures time-based amounts, typically seconds and nanoseconds. Period represents date-based amounts in years, months and days. A month is not a fixed number of seconds, so Period and Duration answer different questions.

sections.heading: Formatting and immutability
sections.body: DateTimeFormatter parses and formats temporal values. The standard formatters are immutable and thread-safe. Date-time objects are immutable; operations such as plusDays return a new value rather than modifying the receiver.

title: Java Concurrency & Threads
overview: Concurrency allows multiple tasks to make progress over overlapping periods. Java threads share heap objects but have per-thread execution stacks, so shared mutable state needs careful coordination.

sections.heading: Creating work
sections.body: A Thread object represents a thread of execution. Calling start schedules a new thread and eventually invokes run on that thread. Calling run directly is an ordinary method call on the current thread. Implementing Runnable separates the task from the thread that executes it.

sections.heading: Lifecycle
sections.body: The Thread.State values are NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING and TERMINATED. RUNNABLE includes a thread that is executing or eligible to execute; Java does not expose a separate RUNNING state.

sections.heading: Race conditions and synchronization
sections.body: A race condition occurs when program correctness depends on unpredictable interleaving. synchronized uses an intrinsic monitor to provide mutual exclusion and memory-visibility guarantees around monitor release/acquisition. Synchronize on a stable lock object and keep critical sections appropriately small.

sections.heading: Hazards
sections.body: Deadlock occurs when threads wait indefinitely for locks held by one another. Consistent lock ordering, avoiding unnecessary nested locks and using higher-level concurrency utilities can reduce risk. Synchronization has costs, so design for correctness first and measure performance.

title: Reflection API
overview: Reflection allows a Java program to inspect metadata about classes, constructors, methods, fields and interfaces at runtime. Frameworks use it for capabilities such as dependency injection, object mapping and persistence metadata discovery.

sections.heading: Obtaining Class objects
sections.body: Class<?> metadata can be obtained with TypeName.class, object.getClass() or Class.forName with a fully qualified class name. Class.forName traditionally loads and initialises a class; loading behaviour should be considered when static initialisers have side effects.

sections.heading: Inspecting members
sections.body: Class provides methods such as getName, getSuperclass, getInterfaces, getDeclaredFields, getDeclaredMethods and getDeclaredConstructors. getDeclared methods include members declared by that class regardless of access level; getMethods includes public methods including inherited ones.

sections.heading: Access and risks
sections.body: Reflection can bypass ordinary compile-time access patterns when permitted, but module boundaries and runtime access checks still apply. Deep reflective access can reduce encapsulation, complicate refactoring and create security or performance concerns. Prefer normal APIs unless runtime metadata is genuinely needed.

title: Introduction to Node.js
overview: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime built around the V8 engine and server-side APIs. It is distinct from Java despite the shared word 'Java' in the names.

sections.heading: Node.js and browser JavaScript
sections.body: Both environments execute JavaScript, but browsers provide web-platform APIs such as DOM and window, while Node.js provides server/runtime APIs such as process, filesystem and networking modules. Node.js does not provide a browser DOM by default.

sections.heading: REPL
sections.body: The Node.js REPL is an interactive Read-Eval-Print Loop for entering JavaScript expressions and observing results. It is commonly started by running node without a script path.

sections.heading: Why it appears in this syllabus
sections.body: The Java syllabus page includes an introductory Node.js session alongside reflection-related framework context. Treat Node.js as a separate runtime topic, not as a Java library or part of the JVM.

title: Spring Framework & Spring MVC
overview: Spring is a Java application framework that provides infrastructure for building applications. Its core container manages objects and their dependencies, while modules support web, data access, transactions and other concerns.

sections.heading: IoC and dependency injection
sections.body: Inversion of Control means application object creation and lifecycle responsibilities are delegated to a container or framework. Dependency Injection is a common form of IoC in which a component receives the collaborators it needs, commonly through constructor parameters.

sections.heading: Architecture and modules
sections.body: The Spring ecosystem includes core/container, context, AOP, data access/transaction, web and testing capabilities. Exact module usage depends on the application. Spring Framework is not identical to Spring Boot; Boot adds opinionated auto-configuration and application packaging conventions.

sections.heading: Spring MVC request flow
sections.body: A typical Spring MVC request reaches the DispatcherServlet, which delegates to handler mappings and a controller. The controller processes the request and returns a model/view or response body; view resolution and message conversion complete the response as appropriate.

sections.heading: Design notes
sections.body: Constructor injection makes required dependencies explicit and helps create immutable components. Keep controllers focused on request handling and move business rules into service components. Configure components consistently and avoid hidden global state.
